\chapter{Head and Hand}
\label{ch:ar-head-and-hand}
\hlchaptermodality{11}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the head and the hand in Arabic.}

Say yad, set it against its near-identical Hebrew twin, and contrast how much further raʾs drifted.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ar{رأس}]{\ar{رأس} (raʾs) — the head}

\label{lesson:AR-C11-ras}



\begin{quote}
One more ancient Semitic root — and a word still hard at work in modern political vocabulary, the same way Latin's \emph{caput} is in English.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The word}
\textbf{\ar{رأس}} (\emph{raʾs}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{head}\textquotedblright{} — an ancient Semitic root, cousin of Hebrew \textbf{\he{ראש}} (\emph{rosh}), the very word inside \textbf{Rosh Hashanah}, \textquotedblleft{}head of the year.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{culture}
Arabic builds \textbf{\ar{رئيس}} (\emph{raʾīs}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{president, chief, head {[}of an organization{]}},\textquotedblright{} directly on this same root — literally \textquotedblleft{}the one who is the head.\textquotedblright{} That's exactly the move English makes with Latin \emph{caput}: \textbf{captain} (\textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{} of a unit), \textbf{capital} (\textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{} city). Different language families, the same very human idea — the person or place \textquotedblleft{}at the head\textquotedblright{} is the one in charge.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}raʾs\textquotedblright{} — head
  \item \textquotedblleft{}raʾīs\textquotedblright{} — president, literally \textquotedblleft{}the head {[}one{]}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the Hebrew cousin — \textquotedblleft{}raʾs / rosh\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ar{رأس}} mean, and what's its Hebrew cousin? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Head\textquotedblright{}} — cousin of \textbf{rosh}, as in Rosh Hashanah.) What word is built on it for \textquotedblleft{}president,\textquotedblright{} and what does it literally mean? (\textbf{\ar{رئيس}} \emph{raʾīs}, \textquotedblleft{}the head {[}one{]}\textquotedblright{} — the same \textquotedblleft{}head = leader\textquotedblright{} idea as English \emph{captain/capital} from Latin \emph{caput}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ar{يد}]{\ar{يد} (yad) — the hand}

\label{lesson:AR-C11-yad}



\begin{quote}
Some words wear their age lightly — worn down, reshaped, disguised. This one hasn't changed much at all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The word}
\textbf{\ar{يد}} (\emph{yad}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{hand}\textquotedblright{} — a short, ancient Semitic root. Its Hebrew cousin is spelled and pronounced almost \textbf{identically}: \textbf{\he{יד}} (\emph{yad}). Where \emph{raʾs/rosh} show a family resemblance, \emph{yad/yad} is closer to twins — one of the more strikingly unchanged shared words across the whole Semitic family.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}yad\textquotedblright{} — hand
  \item the Hebrew twin — \textquotedblleft{}yad\textquotedblright{} — almost the same word
  \item contrast — \textquotedblleft{}raʾs/rosh\textquotedblright{} changed more than \textquotedblleft{}yad/yad\textquotedblright{} did
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ar{يد}} mean? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Hand.\textquotedblright{}}) How does it compare to its Hebrew cousin? (\textbf{Nearly identical} — both \emph{yad} — one of the more strikingly unchanged shared words across the Semitic family.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kayfa ḥāluka? · bi-khayr]{How are you, cold}

\label{lesson:AR-R11-how-are-you-cold}



\begin{quote}
Ask after somebody and answer them back, both parts, without reading on. If the question came out as a memorised noise rather than three pieces you can name, this page is for you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{letters, right to left} & \textbf{what it is} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ar{كيف}} \emph{kayfa} & \emph{kāf · yāʾ · fāʾ} & how — a question word, partner to \textbf{\ar{ما}} \\
\textbf{\ar{حال}} \emph{ḥāl} & \emph{ḥāʾ · alif · lām} & state, condition — root \textbf{ḥ–w–l}, to turn \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The \textbf{\ar{ح}} is the deep throat \emph{ḥ}, not an English \emph{h}. And \textbf{\ar{حال}} is the whole point of the question: English asks after \textbf{you}, Arabic asks after your \textbf{state} — the thing that turns and changes, which is exactly what its root means.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same suffix, one lesson on}]
\textbf{\ar{كيف} \ar{حالك؟}} bolts three pieces you already own together: \emph{how} + \emph{state} + \emph{your}. The suffix behaves identically to the one that gave you \textbf{\ar{اسمي}}, and it splits the same way.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{to a man} & \textbf{to a woman} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ar{كيف} \ar{حالك؟}} \emph{kayfa ḥāluka} & \textbf{\ar{كيف} \ar{حالك؟}} \emph{kayfa ḥāluki} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Literally: \textbf{how — your-state}. No \emph{is}, no \emph{are}. The same zero copula that ran through the name exchange runs through this one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{How to answer: two replies where English has one}
\textbf{\ar{بخير}} \emph{bi-khayr} is \textbf{\ar{بـ}} (\emph{in}) plus \textbf{\ar{خير}} (\emph{khayr}, good) — literally \emph{in goodness}. You had met \emph{khayr} long before you were told: it sits inside the morning greeting \textbf{\ar{صباح} \ar{الخير}}, \emph{morning of the good}.

\textbf{\ar{الحمد} \ar{لله}} \emph{al-ḥamdu lillāh} comes back more often than \emph{bi-khayr} does. Every letter in it is one you can write — \emph{alif, lām, ḥāʾ, mīm, dāl, hāʾ} — and it says \textbf{the praise is to God}, from the root \textbf{ḥ–m–d}, to praise.

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} ask a man — \emph{kayfa ḥāluka?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} ask a woman — \emph{kayfa ḥāluki?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the plain answer — \emph{bi-khayr, shukran}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the commoner answer — \emph{al-ḥamdu lillāh}
  \item \emph{Recall:} the three attaching pieces inside these lines — \emph{al-}, \emph{bi-}, \emph{li-}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the root behind \textbf{\ar{حال}} and what it means. (\textbf{ḥ–w–l}, to turn or change.) Give the literal sense of \textbf{\ar{بخير}}. (\emph{\textbf{In goodness}}.) Give the literal sense of \textbf{\ar{الحمد} \ar{لله}}. (\textbf{The praise is to God}.) And name the question word that partners \textbf{\ar{كيف}}. (\textbf{\ar{ما}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
